`map`, `filter`, and similar methods take a second argument that becomes `this` inside the callback. It sits after the callback, where it is easy to miss. With an arrow function it does nothing, because an arrow function keeps the `this` of the code around it.

The rule checks `every`, `filter`, `find`, `findLast`, `findIndex`, `findLastIndex`, `flatMap`, `forEach`, `map`, and `some`, and the third argument of `Array.from()` and `Array.fromAsync()`.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad */}
```js
const mine = items.filter(function (item) {
  return item.owner === this.id;
}, user);
```

{/* bad */}
```js
const rows = items.map(table.renderRow, table);
```

{/* bad */}
```js
const cards = Array.from(nodes, function (node) {
  return this.wrap(node);
}, view);
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
const mine = items.filter((item) => item.owner === user.id);
const rows = items.map((item) => table.renderRow(item));
const cards = Array.from(nodes, (node) => view.wrap(node));
```

A call is skipped if its first argument cannot be a function. So are library methods with the same names, such as `_.map()`, `R.map()`, `$.map()`, and `React.Children.map()`, because their second argument means something else:

{/* good */}
```js
const match = collection.find("email", address);
const names = _.map(users, formatName);
```
